finding: The site has no live range for this job, so there is nothing to grade; this file is a first build. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks; oil = the maker's capacity in quarts x a per-quart price, plus one filter): economy 2015 Corolla (4.4 qt) about $63-$168; midsize 2016 Camry (4.6 qt) about $64-$170; truck 2016 F-150 5.0L (7.7 qt) about $87-$200; luxury 2015 BMW 328i (5.3 qt) about $76-$236. Against the benchmarks: a chain price survey found full synthetic at $45 (Walmart) to $100 (Valvoline, Firestone Premium), $65 at a local mechanic and $109 at a dealer, and a second article puts Walmart's full synthetic at about $59-$65. So the low end of the build ($63-$87) lands in the middle of real menu prices, while the high end ($168-$236) is well above anything the benchmarks show for an ordinary car. Candidly, that gap is expected: an oil change is sold at a menu price rather than built up from parts and hourly labor, and the menu prices found sit below a build that charges retail or list oil prices plus up to 45 minutes at $160/hr. The build therefore overstates what most drivers pay; the benchmarks ($45-$109 for a full synthetic service that typically includes up to five quarts) are the better guide to a real bill, with extra quarts charged on top for the larger truck fill. How solid the numbers are: the hours are general, not vehicle-specific. No manufacturer-stated oil-change time was found; the low end is a quick-lube chain's own '15 minutes or less' and the high end is two independent repair shops' '30 to 45 minutes'. The oil capacities are meant to be the makers' figures, but no maker's manual page could be loaded directly: the Corolla figure comes from a data sheet that says it was compiled from Toyota owner's manuals plus one guide, and the Camry, F-150 and BMW capacities each rest on one third-party guide. Parts: Toyota oil and filters use genuine list prices from an OEM catalog. No Ford or BMW genuine oil list price could be loaded, so the truck high end is a seller's price for a Motorcraft kit and the luxury high end is a premium aftermarket kit, not OEM list. The BMW oil grade is an open point: the kit sold for this engine is 5W-30, one guide names 0W-20 or 0W-30, so the owner's manual decides. Only two independent benchmark sources were found (the two chain-survey rows come from the same article); the chains' own price pages loaded without prices.
extras: A quote often adds a charge per extra quart beyond the five a menu price usually includes (one survey reports $5-$10 a quart at one chain), which matters for the truck (7.7 quarts) and the BMW (5.3), plus shop supplies and an oil disposal or environmental fee, a new drain plug washer, and sales tax. Many menu prices bundle a tire rotation, fluid top-offs and a multi-point inspection. Engine and cabin air filters, wiper blades and other fluid services are commonly offered at the same visit and priced separately. Cartridge-style filters and under-engine covers can add a little time.
